paragraphs: Friend, here's what I love about this passage. Nobody in it is pretending to be fine. David says, "I am poor and needy," and the second writer says his enemies are saying, "God has forsaken him." Neither one cleans it up for company, and both keep praying anyway (Ps 70:5; 71:11). Bring God the real, messy, no-apron-on version of you, because that's the only version He's asking to hear from.

Now watch what the writer does when the pressure is on. He says, "But I will always hope and will praise You more and more" (Ps 71:14). He isn't praying his way OUT of his troubles first and praising later. He praises right in the middle of them, and he admits he "cannot know their full measure" (Ps 71:15). I think that's the whole trick: you don't need to understand all of God to lean on Him, you just need to keep leaning, like he has "since birth" (Ps 71:6).

And then there's the part that gets me right in the mustache. He's old and gray, and his biggest prayer isn't comfort, it's "until I proclaim Your power to the next generation" (Ps 71:18). Getting older doesn't end your usefulness to God. He still has work for you to do, and somebody coming up behind you needs to hear what you've seen. So tell it, baker, and tell it LOUD. God has "done great things," and there's a whole next generation waiting to hear about them (Ps 71:19).
